name: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital: research (charityevals)
summary: St. Jude spends about $880 million a year on research into childhood cancer and other catastrophic childhood diseases, $720 million of it from its own funds; its cancer research is about a fifth of all childhood cancer research worldwide. For its fiscal year to June 2025 this model credits the cancer research with that share of what a year of the field's research does to the world's childhood cancer burden (11.5 million DALYs a year), anchored on published returns to medical research, and values the non-cancer research (about 30%), which has no outcome measure, at comparable research elsewhere on the site, discounted. The result, about 0.01 years of healthy life per $1,000, is far below the site's global-health median (under a tenth of it) because research pays off only after a long lag, through uptake by others, and the field's progress is shared among all its funders. It is dominated by judgment (the chance a year's research yields an advance and the share of the burden it averts) and its plausible range spans about seventyfold (about 0.0016 to 0.11 years of healthy life per $1,000).

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Programmes with no outcome data
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for a programme that publishes no outcome data at all: it is valued at the result per dollar of the same kind of work elsewhere on the site, read live, and counts less by the shared slider "How much we count a programme we could only estimate from similar ones" (docs/normalization.md 2.12). A programme with some outcome data is modelled from it in the chain above, with wide ranges, never here.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ programme expenses, both net of insurers' and grant money)

Childhood and adolescent cancer, DALYs a year worldwide (ages 0-19)

source.title: Force et al. (GBD 2017 Childhood Cancer Collaborators), The global burden of childhood and adolescent cancer in 2017, Lancet Oncology 2019
source.quote: there were 11.5 million (95% UI 10.6–12.3) DALYs due to childhood cancer

rows.explainer: The burden St. Jude's cancer research addresses, worldwide, since its protocols and drugs travel (82.2% of it in low, low-middle and middle Socio-demographic Index countries, where access, not knowledge, limits survival: share_burden_addressable takes that into account). 97% of it is years of life lost. The study's 95% uncertainty interval is the range; GBD's later rounds put it at about the same.

rows.label: Share of the world's childhood cancer burden one successful year's advance averts once adopted
rows.explainer: Judgment. A typical advance of the kind St. Jude produces (a risk-adapted leukaemia protocol, a targeted drug for one subtype, a better brain-tumour regimen) raises survival by several points for one cancer: in the high-income countries that adopt it at once (18% of the burden) that is a few per cent of their childhood cancer burden, and in middle-income countries, where much of the rest is, it spreads more slowly with the protocols partners adapt. 2% of the world's burden; 0.8% for an advance in a rare cancer, 6% for one in leukaemia or brain tumours that middle-income units take up.

rows.label: Chance that a year of the field's research yields such an advance
rows.explainer: Judgment, so that share_burden_addressable × p_success (0.5% of the world's burden a year at the best guess) matches the research-returns reference class: US childhood cancer mortality fell by about half between 1975 and 2010, about 2% a year, most of it from treatment advances, and the world's falls more slowly; UK cancer research earned a health-gain return of about 10% a year with a lag of about 15 years (Glover et al., BMC Medicine 2014). field_dalys_per_dollar shows the check. A quarter of years bring such an advance; low if most of the year's work is basic science that never reaches practice, high if the year's clinical trials change protocols.

rows.label: Years the field's research brings the advance forward
rows.explainer: Judgment: how much later the advance would come if this year's research weren't done, with others' work going on (Convention 5: the counterfactual question is answered here, so counterfactual_adj is 1). The medical-research reference class (HERG, Office of Health Economics and RAND Europe 2008; Glover 2014) implies a few years; 2 for crowded fields (leukaemia), 10 for rare tumours St. Jude almost alone studies.

rows.label: Years from the funding until the result is in practice
rows.explainer: Judgment on the reference class: about 17 years from research to practice (Morris, Wooding and Grant, J R Soc Med 2011), about 15 for UK cancer research (Glover et al. 2014); St. Jude's spending includes many clinical trials, whose results change protocols within a few years, beside basic science with the long lag. 12 (6-17).

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the result is in practice
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.explainer: Judgment, the family's default (0.7): the chain is built from reference-class returns to research, not from St. Jude's own record traced to practice; St. Jude's record is strong (Total Therapy trials took leukaemia survival from under 10% to over 90%), which is why the discount isn't larger.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: what would have happened without this year's research is in years_brought_forward (Convention 5), so it isn't discounted again.

rows.label: All funders' spending on childhood cancer research a year, worldwide
rows.explainer: Judgment built up from its parts: the US National Cancer Institute 'spent more than $600 million on childhood cancer' in FY2023 (St. Baldrick's, https://blog.stbaldricks.org/?p=36179), St. Jude's own cancer research about $500 million, other US children's hospitals' and charities' own funds (St. Baldrick's, Alex's Lemonade Stand, Dana-Farber, CHOP and others) a few hundred million, Europe and the rest of the world (national research councils, Children with Cancer UK, the Princess Máxima Centre, EU programmes) about $500 million, and drug companies' paediatric trials (required by US and EU paediatric rules) several hundred million.

rows.label: St. Jude's share of the field's research funding
rows.explainer: St. Jude's own cancer research ÷ all funders' childhood cancer research (Convention 2): about a fifth. The NIH grants St. Jude receives are counted in the field, not in St. Jude's share.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

source.title: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital and ALSAC, combined financial statements, years ended June 30, 2025 and 2024 (audited, Deloitte & Touche LLP)
source.page: p. 3, combined statements of financial position (in 000s)
source.quote: CASH AND CASH EQUIVALENTS $ 557,709 ... UNRESTRICTED INVESTMENTS 8,444,862 ... RESTRICTED INVESTMENTS 1,587,521

rows.explainer: Cash ($557.7 million), unrestricted investments ($8,444.9 million) and investments restricted by donors ($1,587.5 million): about three and three-quarter years of spending held in reserve.

rows.label: Years a donation waits before St. Jude spends it
rows.explainer: The reserves ÷ a year's spending, as the template asks for a charity that spends from reserves: 3.7 years. St. Jude holds its reserves by policy and spends from donations, bequests and investment returns, so a dollar given today adds to the pool and is, on average, spent about this much later. While it waits it is invested (interest_yield), which almost cancels the discount.

rows.label: Long-run nominal return on the invested reserves
rows.explainer: Judgment. The reserves earned $939.3 million in FY2025 on about $9.6 billion of investments (p. 4; average of the two year-ends, p. 3), 9.7%, and $856.7 million in FY2024: two strong market years. Long-run returns of diversified endowment portfolios have averaged about 6-7% a year nominal over ten-year periods (US college and university endowment studies, NACUBO-Commonfund); 6.5%, 4% in a weak decade, 9% at the recent returns.

rows.label: Yearly rise in the cost of care and research
rows.explainer: Judgment: US medical-care prices have risen about 3% a year over the past two decades (BLS consumer price index for medical care), a little faster than general inflation; what a dollar held in reserve buys later falls by this much a year.

rows.label: Real return on the invested reserves while a donation waits
rows.explainer: The return in what it buys: the benefit a later dollar buys is valued in today's care.

rows.label: Discount for the years a donation waits in the reserves
rows.explainer: The same wait as in the patient care model: a donation joins the reserves and is spent about 3.7 years later, earning the real return meanwhile.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above, with the reserves' wait.

rows.label: Other effects not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Judgment: open data and tools (St. Jude Cloud, the Pediatric Cancer Genome Project) used by researchers elsewhere, and survivorship research that cuts late effects for the survivors of every centre (positive); results that don't replicate (negative, mostly in evidence_adj already).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The other effects, as one share.

rows.label: Years of healthy life per dollar
The whole field's research: healthy years per dollar, before St. Jude's share and the donor steps (for reading)
rows.explainer: A check against the reference class: what a dollar of all funders' childhood cancer research does in this chain, about what UK cancer research's return implies: Glover et al. (2014) attribute about 1 million QALYs (17% of the 5.9 million gained 1991-2010) to roughly £5 billion of UK cancer research done about 15 years earlier, some 2e-4 QALYs a pound undiscounted, about 4-6e-5 a dollar in today's dollars once the 15-year wait is discounted at the shared rate; this row is about 5e-5.

rows.label: Spending on programmes with no outcome data: St. Jude's non-cancer research, FY2025
rows.explainer: The non-cancer research paid from St. Jude's own funds (blood disorders including sickle cell gene therapy, infectious diseases including the WHO collaborating centre for influenza, neurobiology, structural biology): about $216 million. St. Jude publishes no outcome measure for it that the chain above could use, so it is valued at comparable research elsewhere on the site, discounted (Convention 12). Not part of program_spend.

rows.label: Result per dollar of comparable programmes on the site (units of value per dollar you give)
rows.explainer: The nearest evaluated research programme on the site: Breast Cancer Now's research (SoGive's model, read live), the one ranked medical-research charity model; the motor neurone disease and arthritis models are upper bounds, not estimates. Not St. Jude's own cancer research model, which would value the non-cancer research by the same judgments it was meant to test.

rows.label: Share of the programme spending here that has no outcome data
rows.explainer: The modelled programmes' result counts for the rest of the spending.

rows.label: Units of value per dollar you give, from programmes with no outcome data
rows.explainer: Comparable programmes' result for this share of the spending, counted less by the shared slider: missing data is always discounted, the same way in every model.

rows.label: The same, in this model's unit (DALYs)
rows.explainer: The bridge from units of value into this model's unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6); the unit's conversion cancels it, so these programmes count exactly their peers' value. Don't edit it.
